## Introduction

**Wind energy in Finland is growing fast**

- In 2024, wind produced **24% of Finland's electricity**
- Grid operators need accurate short-term forecasts for scheduling

**Why federated learning?**

- Raw station data may be commercially sensitive: centralized training is not always possible
- Stations share weather patterns; neighbors could help each other learn better models
- FL enables collaboration **without sharing raw data**

**Gap:** FL for wind speed over dense public meteorological networks is largely unexplored.
Prior work (Li et al., 2023) focuses on small private wind farm networks.

**Question:** Does collaborating over a station graph improve next-hour wind speed forecasts?

::: {.notes}
- grid operators can burn coal or other non-renewable energy sources based on predicted demand.
:::

---

## Problem Formulation

**Each node = one FMI weather station** (136 stations, filtered to ≥80% hourly completeness)

**Prediction target:** Next-hour wind speed $\hat{y}^{(i)}_t = ws^{(i)}_{t+1}$

**Features** (6 per station):

$$\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_t = \bigl[ws_{t-3},\ ws_{t-2},\ ws_{t-1},\ ta_{t-1},\ rh_{t-1},\ pa_{t-1}\bigr]^\top$$

Lagged wind speeds capture temporal autocorrelation; pressure gradients drive surface wind; temperature and humidity correlate with large-scale weather patterns like storms

**Local model:** Linear regression $\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^{(i)\top} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}$, $\mathbf{w}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^7$: chosen because each station has abundant data and only 6 features

**Loss: MSE:** differentiable everywhere, closed-form gradient, penalizes large errors quadratically

Both features and labels are **z-score normalized** using training statistics only

::: {.notes}
- Each node is one FMI station; filtered to 136 stations with at least 80% completeness
- Target: next-hour wind speed
- 6 features: 3 lagged wind speeds (temporal autocorrelation) + pressure, temperature, humidity
- Linear model: justified by abundant data (6,000+ hours) and only 6 features
- MSE: differentiable, closed-form gradient, quadratic penalty on large errors
- Z-score normalization using training stats only; prevents data leakage
:::

---

## Graph Topologies

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**System 1: Geographic k-NN**

Connect each station to its $k=5$ closest neighbors (Haversine distance)

Edge weights via Gaussian kernel: closer stations get stronger weights:
$$A_{ij} = \exp\!\left(\frac{-d_{ij}^2}{\sigma^2}\right)$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**System 2: Correlation k-NN**

Connect each station to its $k=5$ most correlated neighbors (Pearson on 2024 wind speeds)

Raw correlation as edge weight: captures meteorological similarity beyond geography:
$$A_{ij} = \text{corr}(ws^{(i)}, ws^{(j)}),\quad A_{ij} \geq 0$$
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- System 1: connect to 5 geographically closest neighbors; Gaussian weights favor closer stations
- System 2: connect to 5 most correlated neighbors by Pearson correlation on wind speeds
- Correlation can capture meteorological similarity beyond geography (e.g. two distant coastal stations)
:::

## Data

**Source:** FMI Open Data, hourly observations for all of 2024

**Variables:** wind speed, air temperature, relative humidity, atmospheric pressure

**Quality filter:** 202 FMI stations, filtered to $\geq 80\%$ hourly completeness: 165 stations remain

- Small gaps ($\leq 2$ h) filled by linear interpolation; larger gaps dropped
- 29 stations lack data for one or more non-wind variables entirely and are excluded: **136 stations**

**Chronological train/val/test split** (no data leakage):

| Split | Fraction | Purpose |
|-------|----------|---------|
| Train | 70% | Fit model weights |
| Validation | 15% | Select $\alpha$ |
| Test | 15% | Final evaluation |

::: {.notes}
- FMI Open Data: 4 variables, hourly, full year 2024
- 136 stations after 80% completeness filter
- Short gaps interpolated; longer gaps dropped
- Chronological split: shuffling would leak future data into training
- Validation set used only for selecting alpha
:::

---

## Methodology: GTVMin + FedGD

**GTVMin objective:** balance local fit vs. inter-station agreement:

$$\min_{\mathbf{w}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{w}^{(n)}} \sum_{i=1}^{n} L_i(\mathbf{w}^{(i)}) + \alpha \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}} A_{ij} \|\mathbf{w}^{(i)} - \mathbf{w}^{(j)}\|^2$$

GTV penalty uses squared $\ell_2$ norm: smooth, closed-form gradient, strongly convex for $\alpha > 0$

**FedGD update** (synchronous, all nodes update simultaneously):

$$\mathbf{w}^{(i)} \leftarrow \mathbf{w}^{(i)} - \eta\Bigl[\color{#f39c12}{\nabla L_i(\mathbf{w}^{(i)})} + \color{#1abc9c}{2\alpha \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} A_{ij}\left(\mathbf{w}^{(i)} - \mathbf{w}^{(j)}\right)}\Bigr]$$

- [local gradient]{style="color: #f39c12;"}: pull weights toward the station's own data
- [disagreement penalty]{style="color: #1abc9c;"}: pull weights toward neighbors, weighted by edge strength

Only **model parameters** are shared; raw data never leaves the node

Hyperparameters: $\eta = 0.01$, 750 iterations, $\mathbf{w}^{(i)}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01)$

::: {.notes}
- GTVMin: local MSE loss + graph total variation penalty on parameter disagreement
- Squared L2 norm: smooth, closed-form gradient, strongly convex (unique minimizer)
- FedGD: first highlight the local gradient term, then the disagreement term
- All nodes update simultaneously; only weights are communicated, not raw data
:::

---

## Selecting $\alpha$

![](figures/alpha_sweep-1.png){width=55%}

Both systems select $\alpha^* = 0.1$: **weak collaboration is optimal**

Strong collaboration ($\alpha \geq 1$) hurts: local models are already well-specified

::: {.notes}
- Sweep over alpha candidates using validation MSE
- Both systems pick alpha = 0.1: only weak collaboration helps
- Performance degrades at alpha >= 1: a first sign local models don't need neighbors
:::

---

## Results

| System | $\alpha$ | Train MSE | Val MSE | Test MSE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline ($\alpha=0$) | 0.00 | 0.2345 | 0.2381 | 0.2638 |
| System 1 (Geographic) | 0.10 | 0.2347 | 0.2377 | 0.2630 |
| System 2 (Correlation) | 0.10 | 0.2349 | 0.2377 | **0.2628** |

All three systems perform nearly identically: FL provides negligible improvement

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](figures/convergence-1.png){width=80%}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](figures/node_boxplot-1.png){width=80%}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- All three systems achieve nearly identical test MSE; improvement is ~0.001
- Convergence curves: all systems converge smoothly to the same level
- Boxplot: FL neither rescues worst-performing stations nor degrades the best
:::

---

## Per-Station Analysis

![](figures/pred_vs_actual-1.png){width=55%}

- Worst-fitting stations have **higher wind speed variability**, not worse models
- FL neither rescues outlier stations nor degrades the best-performing ones

::: {.notes}
- Scatter in predictions comes from high wind speed variability, not model failure
- FL cannot fix this: it is a data characteristic, not a modeling problem
:::

---

## Conclusion

**FL provided no practical benefit** over the local baseline in this setting

**Why?** The local model is already well-specified:

- 136 stations x ~6,000 training hours = abundant local data
- A 7-parameter linear model (6 features + bias) leaves little room for graph regularization to help
- $\alpha = 0.1$ confirms that strong collaboration is harmful

**Limitations and future directions:**

- Linear models may be too simple: try shallow MLP or LSTM local models
- A full year of data reduces the value of borrowing: test in sparser data regimes
- Symmetric k-NN graphs miss asymmetric propagation: try wind-flow-aware directed graphs

::: {.notes}
- Both FL systems gave negligible improvement over the local baseline
- Root cause: abundant data + simple linear model = already well-specified locally
- Alpha = 0.1 confirms neighbors add little value
- Each limitation points directly to a future direction
:::
